nodes.name: NP-hardness of maximum temporal connected component
nodes.statement: As observed by~\textcite{BF03}, the fact that \emph{(temporally) connected components} do not form equivalence classes and intersect in non trivial ways implies, among other consequences, that finding one of maximum size is NP-hard.
conclusions: finding one of maximum size is NP-hard
nodes.statement_short: Finding a maximum-size temporally connected component is NP-hard.

nodes.name: Erdős-Rényi random graph G_{n,p}
nodes.statement:
An Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} random graph $G_{n,p}$ is obtained by placing an edge between each distinct pair
of~$n$~vertices
\footnote{We use the terms \emph{vertex} and \emph{node} interchangeably.}
independently with probability $p$.

nodes.name: Temporal connectivity thresholds in temporal Erdős-Rényi graphs
nodes.statement:
Namely, at $p=\log n/n$, any \emph{fixed} pair of
vertices can asymptotically almost surely (\aas) reach each other; at $2\log n/n$, at least one
vertex (and in fact, any fixed vertex) can \aas reach all the others;
and at $3\log n/n$, \aas all the vertices can reach all others, i.e.,\xspace
the graph is temporally connected.
conclusions: at $p=\log n/n$, any \emph{fixed} pair of vertices can asymptotically almost surely (\aas) reach each other
nodes.statement_short: Thresholds log n/n (fixed pair), 2 log n/n (one source), 3 log n/n (temporal connectivity) in the temporal ER model.

nodes.name: Main Theorem (informal)
conclusions: $o(n)$ \aas
$n-o(n)$ \aas
$o(n)$ \aas
$n-o(n)$ \aas

nodes.statement_short: Largest temporally connected component in temporal ER graph jumps from o(n) to n-o(n) at p = log n/n.

nodes.name: Giant component evolution in Erdős-Rényi graphs
nodes.statement:
Below a
critical probability $p_0=1/n$, almost all the components are trees,
and no component is larger than $O(\log n)$. Then, at~$p_0$, a
single ``giant'' component of size $\Theta(n^{2/3})$ arises. Then, at
$p = c/n > 1/n$, this component contains a constant fraction~$1-x/c$
of all vertices (with $0 < x < 1$ being defined through $xe^{-x} = ce^{-c}$).
As soon as $p\in\omega(1/n)$, the component contains all but $o(n)$
vertices.
conclusions: As soon as $p\in\omega(1/n)$, the component contains all but $o(n)$ vertices.
nodes.statement_short: Static ER: components O(log n) below 1/n, giant Θ(n^{2/3}) at 1/n, linear above, n-o(n) once p ∈ ω(1/n).

nodes.name: Giant strongly connected component in directed random graphs
nodes.statement:
Namely, for $p= c/n < 1/n$, a.a.s.\ all strongly connected components have size less than $3c^{-2}\log n$, and when $p= c/n > 1/n$, the graph contains a strongly connected component of size approximately
$\left(1- x/c\right)^2n$ (with $x$~as above)~\cite{Karp1990,frieze_karonski_2015}, which implies that this component contains all but $o(n)$ vertices when $p\in\omega(1/n)$.
conclusions: the graph contains a strongly connected component of size approximately $\left(1- x/c\right)^2n$
nodes.statement_short: Directed random graphs: SCCs of size O(log n) below 1/n, giant SCC of size ≈(1-x/c)^2 n above.

nodes.name: Interval notation [k], [a,b]
nodes.statement: In this paper, $[k]$ denotes the set of integers $\{1, \ldots, k\}$, and $[a, b]$ denotes either the discrete interval from $a$ to $b$, or the continuous interval from $a$ to $b$, the distinction being clear from the context.

nodes.name: Vertex and edge set V(G), E(G)
nodes.statement: For a graph $G$, we denote by $V(G)$ and $E(G)$ its vertex set and edge set respectively.

nodes.name: Minimum and maximum degree
nodes.statement: We denote by $\delta(G)$ and $\Delta(G)$ the minimum and the maximum vertex degree of $G$ respectively.

nodes.name: Complete graph K_n
nodes.statement: As usual, $K_n$ denotes the complete $n$-vertex graph.

nodes.name: Temporal graph
nodes.statement:
A \emph{temporal graph} is a pair $(G, \lambda)$, where $G=(V,E)$ is a \emph{static} graph and $\lambda$ is a function
that assigns to every edge $e \in E$ a finite set of numbers, interpreted as presence times.
also_stated_at: A temporal graph is a pair $\mathcal G = (G, \lambda)$, where $G=(V,E)$ is an \emph{underlying} (static) graph, and $\lambda$ is an \emph{edge labeling function} that assigns to every edge~$e \in E$ a set of time labels $\lambda(e) \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ indicating when this edge is present.

nodes.name: Underlying graph and time labels
nodes.statement:
The graph $G$
is called the \emph{underlying graph} of the temporal graph and the elements of $\lambda(e)$ are called the \emph{time labels} of $e$.

nodes.name: Notation (V,E,λ) for temporal graphs
nodes.statement:
Instead of $(G, \lambda)$ we will sometimes use the notation
$(V,E, \lambda)$ to denote the same temporal graph.

nodes.name: Simple temporal graph
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, in this paper, we restrict our consideration only to \emph{simple} temporal graphs\footnote{We remark that all our results can be directly transferred to another, closely related model of non-simple temporal graphs; see Section 6.1.2 in \cite{CasteigtsRRZ21}.},
i.e., temporal graphs in which every edge $e \in E$ is only present at a single point in time, i.e., $|\lambda(e)| = 1$.
differentia: every edge $e \in E$ is only present at a single point in time

nodes.name: Vertex and edge set of a temporal graph
nodes.statement: We sometimes write $V(\mathcal{G})$ and $E(\mathcal{G})$ for the node and edge set of a temporal graph $\mathcal{G}$ respectively.

nodes.name: Temporal subgraph
nodes.statement: A temporal graph $\mathcal{H}=(V_{\mathcal{H}}, E_{\mathcal{H}}, \lambda_{\mathcal{H}})$ is a \emph{temporal subgraph} of a temporal graph $\mathcal{G}=(V_{\mathcal{G}}, E_{\mathcal{G}}, \lambda_{\mathcal{G}})$, if $V_{\mathcal{H}}\subseteq V_{\mathcal{G}}$, $E_{\mathcal{H}}\subseteq E_{\mathcal{G}}$ and $\lambda_{\mathcal{H}}(e)=\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}(e)$ for all $e\in E_{\mathcal{H}}$.

nodes.name: Induced temporal subgraph G[S]
nodes.statement:
For a vertex set $S \subseteq V(\mathcal G)$, we denote by $\mathcal G[S]$ a temporal subgraph of $\mathcal G$
induced by $S$.

nodes.name: Time-window subgraph G_[a,b]
nodes.statement: We use $\mathcal{G}_{[a,b]}$ to denote the temporal subgraph of $\mathcal{G}$ with the same node set $V_{\mathcal{G}}$, the edge set $E':=\{e\in E_{\mathcal{G}}:\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}(e)\in [a,b]\}$, and the time labeling function $\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}|_{E'}$ which is the restriction of $\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}$ to $E'$.
nodes.statement_short: G_[a,b] keeps all vertices and only the edges with time labels in [a,b].

nodes.name: Temporal (u,v)-path
nodes.statement:
A \emph{temporal $(u, v)$-path} in $\mathcal{G}=(V, E, \lambda)$ between two nodes $u,v\in V$ is a sequence $u=u_0,u_1,\ldots, u_\ell=v$ such that $e_i=\{u_{i-1}, u_i\}\in E$ for each $i\in [\ell]$,
and time labels are increasing, i.e., $\lambda(e_1)< \ldots < \lambda(e_\ell)$.

nodes.name: Arrival time
nodes.statement: We call $\lambda(e_\ell)$ the \emph{arrival time} of the path.

nodes.name: Foremost (u,v)-path
nodes.statement: A temporal $(u,v)$-path is called \emph{foremost $(u, v)$-path} if it has the earliest arrival time among all temporal $(u,v)$-paths.
differentia: it has the earliest arrival time among all temporal $(u,v)$-paths

nodes.name: Temporal reachability
nodes.statement: If there exists a temporal $(u,v)$-path, we say that $u$ can reach $v$ (every vertex reaches itself).

nodes.name: Set reaching a vertex
nodes.statement: A set~$S \subseteq V$ is said to \emph{reach~$v$} if at least one of its elements reaches~$v$.

nodes.name: Foremost (S,v)-path
nodes.statement: In that case, a \emph{foremost $(S, v)$-path} in $\mathcal{G}$ is a temporal $(u, v)$-path with earliest arrival time among all $u\in S$.

nodes.name: Temporal source
nodes.statement: A vertex $u\in V$ is called \emph{temporal source} in $\mathcal{G}=(V, E, \lambda)$ if there exists a temporal $(u,v)$-path for each $v\in V$.

nodes.name: Temporal sink
nodes.statement: Similarly, a vertex $v\in V$ is called \emph{temporal sink} in $\mathcal{G}$ if there exists a temporal $(u,v)$-path for each $u\in V$.

nodes.name: Temporally connected
nodes.statement: A temporal graph $\mathcal{G}=(V, E, \lambda)$ is \emph{temporally connected} if all nodes are temporal sources.

nodes.name: Open temporally connected component
nodes.statement:
An \emph{open temporally connected component} or simply \emph{connected component} in $\mathcal{G}$ is an inclusion-wise maximal set $Z\subseteq V$
of nodes such that for every ordered pair of vertices $u,v\in Z$, there exists a temporal $(u,v)$-path in $\mathcal{G}$.
differentia: for every ordered pair of vertices $u,v\in Z$, there exists a temporal $(u,v)$-path in $\mathcal{G}$
also_stated_at: If the vertices of the component need temporal paths traveling \emph{outside} the component in order to reach each other, then the component is \emph{open}; otherwise, it is \emph{closed} \cite{BF03}.

nodes.name: Closed connected component
nodes.statement:
If for every ordered pair $u,v\in Z$, there exists a temporal $(u,v)$-path in $\mathcal{G}[Z]$, then $Z$ is called
\emph{closed connected component}.

nodes.name: Temporal Erdős-Rényi random graph
nodes.statement:
An $n$-vertex temporal Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} random graph with the parameter $p \in [0,1]$ is obtained by first drawing a \emph{static} random Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} $G_{n,p}$ and then defining a temporal order on its
edges by ordering them according to a uniformly random permutation.
also_stated_at: In this model, which we refer to as the \emph{temporal Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} random graph model}, a random temporal graph is obtained from an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} random graph $G_{n,p}$ by assigning to each edge a unique label (presence time) according to a uniformly random permutation of its edges.

nodes.name: Model F_{n,p}
nodes.statement:
An equivalent and technically more convenient way of defining the temporal order on the edges is to draw, for every edge $e$, independently and uniformly at random a time label
$\lambda(e)$ from the unit interval $[0,1]$. Since the event that two edges get the same time label happens with probability 0,
all edge orderings induced by such random time labels are equiprobable. Therefore, as long as the absolute values of time labels are irrelevant (which is the case for the questions studied in \cite{CasteigtsRRZ21} and in the present paper), the two models are indeed equivalent. This latter model is denoted as $\mathcal F_{n,p}$.
nodes.statement_short: F_{n,p}: each edge of G_{n,p} gets an independent uniform label in [0,1]; equivalent to a uniform random edge order.

nodes.name: Generating F_{n,p} by restricting F_{n,1}
nodes.statement:
A possible way of generating objects from $\mathcal F_{n,p}$ is to first draw a temporal graph $\mathcal G=(G, \lambda)$ from $\mathcal F_{n,1}$ (thus the underlying graph $G$ is complete), and to then
consider $\mathcal G' = (G',\lambda') = (G,\lambda)|_{[0,p]}$, i.e., the temporal graph obtained from $\mathcal G$ by removing edges
with time labels greater than $p$. Observe that $G' \sim G_{n,p}$ and each time label $\lambda(e)$ is uniformly distributed
on $[0,p]$. Hence, $\mathcal G'$ is distributed according to $\mathcal F_{n,p}$ up to multiplying all labels by a factor of $\frac{1}{p}$, which we can ignore as it neither changes the relative order of time labels nor the absolute values of time labels are of any importance to us.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting a temporal graph from F_{n,1} to labels in [0,p] yields F_{n,p} up to rescaling.

nodes.name: Time-window subgraph is distributed as F_{n,b-a}
nodes.statement: For similar reasons, for any $0 \leq a \leq b \leq 1$, up to rescaling time labels, the temporal subgraph $\mathcal G|_{[a,b]}$ is distributed according to $\mathcal F_{n,q}$, where $q=b-a$.
conclusions: up to rescaling time labels, the temporal subgraph $\mathcal G|_{[a,b]}$ is distributed according to $\mathcal F_{n,q}$, where $q=b-a$

nodes.name: Random temporal graph model F_p(G)
nodes.statement:
For an $n$-vertex graph $G$ and a real value $p\in [0,1]$, we denote by $\mathcal{F}_p(G)$ the following random temporal graph model. A random temporal graph $\mathcal{G}=(V, E, \lambda) \sim \mathcal{F}_p(G)$ is obtained by
(1) independently and uniformly sampling a time label $\lambda'(e)\in [0,1]$ for every $e\in E(G)$, and
(2) setting $V=V(G)$, $E:=\{e\in E(G):\lambda(e)\le p\}$ and $\lambda(e) = \lambda'(e)$ for every $e\in E$.
nodes.statement_short: F_p(G): each edge of base graph G gets an i.i.d. uniform label in [0,1] and is kept iff its label is at most p.

nodes.name: Base graph
nodes.statement: We call $G$ the \emph{base graph} of $\mathcal{F}_p(G)$.

nodes.name: F_{n,p} is F_p(K_n)

Then an arbitrary node in $\mathcal{G}$ is a temporal source with probability at least $1 - n^{-\frac{\alpha^2(2\beta -1)}{2} + 1}$.

conclusions: an arbitrary node in $\mathcal{G}$ is a temporal source with probability at least $1 - n^{-\frac{\alpha^2(2\beta -1)}{2} + 1}$

nodes.name: Increasing temporal forest
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{G}=(V, E, \lambda)$ be a temporal graph and let $S\subseteq V$ be a set of vertices.
	The graph $\mathcal{G}_F=(V_F, E_F, \lambda_F)$ is an \emph{increasing temporal forest for $S$}, if
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
	\item $\mathcal{G}_F$ is a temporal subgraph of $\mathcal{G}$,
	\item the graph $F=(V_F, E_F)$ is a forest (i.e.\ acyclic graph) with $|S|$ components,
	\item for each $s \in S$ there is a connected component~$T_s$ of~$F$ such that $s$~reaches all vertices of~$T_s$ in~$\mathcal{G}_F$.
	\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A temporal subforest with |S| components, each rooted at some s∈S that reaches all its vertices.
nodes.label: def: increasing temporal forest

nodes.name: (Partial) foremost forest / foremost tree
also_stated_at: A \emph{foremost forest for $S$ in $\mathcal G$} is a minimal temporal subgraph that preserves foremost reachabilities from $S$ to all other vertices reachable from $S$ in $\mathcal G$.
nodes.statement_short: Increasing temporal forest whose tree paths are foremost paths from S, covering every vertex reachable from S.
nodes.label: def: foremost forest

nodes.name: Analogy with Prim's algorithm
nodes.statement: The idea of the algorithm similar to Prim's algorithm for minimum spanning trees in static graphs: Starting from $\mathcal{G}_F=(V_F,E_F, \lambda_F)=(S, \emptyset, \emptyset)$, which is trivially a partial foremost forest for $S$, the algorithm iteratively adds one node and one edge to $V_F$ and $E_F, \lambda_F$, respectively, until $\mathcal{G}_F$ becomes a foremost forest for $S$. The main difference to Prim's algorithm is that, in every iteration, the next edge to be added is chosen as the edge of minimum time label among all edges that extend the current increasing temporal forest.
nodes.statement_short: Like Prim's MST algorithm, but always adds the minimum-label edge that extends the increasing temporal forest.

nodes.name: Adding an edge G_F ∪ e
nodes.statement: We write $\mathcal{G}_F \cup e$ for adding the edge $e=\{u, v\}$ to $\mathcal{G}_F$, i.e., the result is the temporal graph $(V_F\cup\{u, v\}, E_F\cup\{e\}, \lambda_F\cup \{(e, \lambda(e))\})$.

nodes.name: Extending edge set ext(G_F)
nodes.statement:
The set of edges that extend the current partial forest can then be defined as
\begin{align*}
	\mathrm{ext}(\mathcal{G}_F)
	:=\{e=\{u,v\}\in E:
                u\in V_F, v\in V\setminus V_F,\text{ and } \mathcal{G}_F\cup e\text{ is an increasing temporal} \\ \text{forest for }S
		\}.
\end{align*}

nodes.name: Foremost Forest algorithm
input: Simple temporal graph $\mathcal{G}=(V, E, \lambda)$; set of nodes $S\subseteq V$.
nodes.statement_short: Grow a forest from S by repeatedly adding the minimum-label edge that extends the increasing temporal forest.
nodes.label: alg: foremost forest

nodes.name: Initialize forest with S
While extending edges exist
Pick minimum-label extending edge
nodes.statement: $e_k := arg\,min \{ \lambda(e) \mid e \in \mathrm{ext}(\mathcal{G}^{k-1}_F)\}$
nodes.statement_short: Select the extending edge of minimum time label

nodes.name: Add edge to forest
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{G}^k_F := \mathcal{G}^{k-1}_F \cup e_k$

nodes.name: Return forest
nodes.statement: \Return{$\mathcal{G}^k_F$}

nodes.name: Foremost Forest Algorithm Correctness
nodes.statement: {\normalfont (Foremost Forest Algorithm Correctness)}\textbf{.} Let $\mathcal{G}=(V, E, \lambda)$ be a simple temporal graph and let $S\subseteq V$ be a set of nodes. Let $k$ be the final value of $k$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg: foremost forest} and let $\mathcal{G}^k_F$ be the temporal graph output by the algorithm. Then (i) $\mathcal{G}^k_F$ is a foremost forest for $S$ in $\mathcal{G}$ and (ii) $\lambda(e_{|S|}) \leq \ldots \leq \lambda(e_{k})$.

$S\subseteq V$ be a set of nodes

(ii) $\lambda(e_{|S|}) \leq \ldots \leq \lambda(e_{k})$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement:
In order to prove (i) we first observe that clearly $\mathcal{G}_F^k$ is an increasing temporal forest for $S$. Thus, in order to show that $\mathcal{G}_F^k$ is a foremost forest for $S$, it remains to prove that,
  \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
    \item $\mathcal{G}_F^k$ is a partial foremost forest, i.e., for all $v\in V(\mathcal{G}_F^k) \setminus S$, the unique temporal $(S, v)$-path in $\mathcal{G}_F^k$ is a foremost $(S, v)$-path in $\mathcal{G}$
    \item $\mathcal{G}_F^k$ is a foremost forest, i.e., $V(\mathcal{G}_F^k)=\{v\in V: \exists (u, v)\text{-temporal path in $G$ for some }u\in S\}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  We start by showing (a) by induction, i.e., we show for $\ell\in [|S|-1, k]$ that, for all $v\in V(\mathcal{G}_F^\ell) \setminus S$, the unique temporal $(S, v)$-path in $\mathcal{G}_F^\ell$ is a foremost $(S, v)$-path in $\mathcal{G}$.
  The statement is obvious for $\ell=|S|-1$. Now, let $|S| \leq \ell \leq k$ and assume the statement holds for $\ell-1$.
  
  Let $e_\ell = \{a,b\}$ be the edge added to $\mathcal{G}^{\ell - 1}_F$ to form $\mathcal{G}^{\ell}_F$, where $a \in V(\mathcal{G}^{\ell - 1}_F)$ and $b \in V\setminus V(\mathcal{G}^{\ell - 1}_F)$.
  As $b$ is the unique node in $V(\mathcal{G}^{\ell}_F)\setminus V(\mathcal{G}^{\ell - 1}_F)$, we only need to show that the temporal
  $(S,b)$-path in $\mathcal{G}^{\ell}_F$ is a foremost $(S,b)$-path in $\mathcal{G}$.
  Suppose that it is not, and let $P$ be a foremost $(S,b)$-path in $\mathcal{G}$. Let $e'$ be the first edge of $P$ with one endpoint in $V(\mathcal{G}^{\ell - 1}_F)$ and the other endpoint not in $V(\mathcal{G}^{\ell - 1}_F)$.
  Clearly, $\mathcal{G}^{\ell - 1}_F \cup e'$ is an increasing temporal forest for $S$ and thus $e'\in \mathrm{ext}(\mathcal{G}^{\ell - 1}_F)$. Furthermore, since $P$ is a foremost $(S, b)$-path in $\mathcal{G}$ and the temporal $(S, b)$-path in $\mathcal{G}_F^{\ell}$ is not, the arrival time of $P$ and thus $\lambda(e')$ is strictly less than $\lambda(e_\ell)$, contradicting the minimal choice of $e_\ell$.
  In order to prove (b), first note that clearly $V(\mathcal{G}_F^k)\subseteq\{v\in V: \exists (u, v)\text{-temporal path in $G$ for some }u\in S\}$. Now, assume for contradiction that there exists a node $v\in V\setminus V(\mathcal{G}_F^k)$ such that there exists a $(u, v)$-temporal path $P$ in $\mathcal{G}$ for some $u\in S$. Similar to before let $e=\{a,b\}$ be the first edge of $P$ with one endpoint in $V(\mathcal{G}^{k}_F)$ and the other endpoint not in $V(\mathcal{G}^{k}_F)$.
  Then, clearly, $e\in \mathrm{ext}(\mathcal{G}_F^k)$, contradicting termination of the algorithm.

  In order to prove (ii), assume that it does not hold and let $\ell \geq 2$ be the minimum index such that
  $\lambda(e_\ell) < \lambda(e_{\ell-1})$. Again, let $e_\ell = \{a,b\}$ and assume that $a \in V(\mathcal{G}_F^{\ell - 1})$ and $b \in V\setminus V(\mathcal{G}_F^{\ell - 1})$, and  let $e_i$ be the last edge of the $(S,a)$-path in $\mathcal{G}_F^{\ell - 1}$.
  Clearly $\lambda(e_i) < \lambda(e_\ell)$ because $\mathcal{G}_F^{\ell}$ is an increasing temporal forest. Hence, $e_i \neq e_{\ell - 1}$ and we obtain that both $e_\ell$ and $e_{\ell -1}$ are in $\mathrm{ext}(\mathcal{G}_F^{\ell - 2})$, a contradiction to the minimum choice of $e_{\ell -1}$.

nodes.statement_short: Induction on iterations with an exchange/contradiction argument against the minimal choice of the added edge.

nodes.name: Foremost Forest Target Set Reachability
nodes.statement:
Let
  \begin{itemize}
    \item $G$ be a graph of minimum degree $\delta(G)\ge n - (\log n)^a$ for some $a\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$,
    \item let $S$ and $T$ be two sets of nodes in $G$ of cardinalities $s\in [(\log n)^{13}, n/2]$ and $t$, respectively,
    \item let $z=z(n)$ be a function with $\varepsilon\le z(n)\le 1 - \varepsilon$ for some constant $\varepsilon\in (0, 1)$, and
    \item let $\mathcal{G}\sim \mathcal{F}_{p}(G)$ with $p\ge \frac{z\log n -\log s}{n} +\frac{3\log\log n}{n}$.
  \end{itemize}
  Then the foremost forest algorithm from $S$ on $\mathcal{G}$ reaches
  $T$ with probability at least $1-\frac{5}{2}n^{-\log\log n} - e^{-\frac{t}{2n}(n^z-s)}$.

$S$ and $T$ be two sets of nodes in $G$ of cardinalities $s\in [(\log n)^{13}, n/2]$ and $t$, respectively
$z=z(n)$ be a function with $\varepsilon\le z(n)\le 1 - \varepsilon$ for some constant $\varepsilon\in (0, 1)$
conclusions: the foremost forest algorithm from $S$ on $\mathcal{G}$ reaches $T$ with probability at least $1-\frac{5}{2}n^{-\log\log n} - e^{-\frac{t}{2n}(n^z-s)}$

nodes.statement: In this section, we globally assume that $s\ge (\log n)^b$ for some constant $b\ge a + 1$.

nodes.name: Edges computed by the algorithm e^S_k
nodes.statement: We denote the edges computed by the algorithm by $e^S_{s},\ldots, e^S_{n-s-1}$.

nodes.name: Random variables Y^S_k and forest process
nodes.statement_short: Y^S_k is the label of the k-th edge added by the foremost forest algorithm from S; E^S_k are candidate crossing edges.

nodes.name: Waiting time X^S_k
nodes.statement:
For $k\in [s, n-s-1]$, let $X^S_k$ be a random variable equal to $Y^S_k - Y^S_{k-1}$,
i.e., to the \emph{waiting time} between the edges $e^S_{k-1}$ and $e^S_k$.

nodes.name: Bounds on |E^S_k| and definition of δ_k
nodes.statement:
We note that our assumption on the minimum degree of the base graph $G$ implies the following inequalities on the size of $|E^S_k|$, $k\in [s, n-s-1]$:
\[
    k \cdot (n - k)
    \ge |E^S_k|
    \ge k \cdot (n-k-\log^a n)
    = (1-\delta_k)\cdot k \cdot (n - k).
\]
where $\delta_k:=\frac{(\log n)^a}{n-k}$.
assumptions: our assumption on the minimum degree of the base graph $G$
conclusions: k \cdot (n - k) \ge |E^S_k| \ge k \cdot (n-k-\log^a n) = (1-\delta_k)\cdot k \cdot (n - k).
nodes.statement_short: Min degree n-(log n)^a gives (1-δ_k)k(n-k) ≤ |E^S_k| ≤ k(n-k), with δ_k=(log n)^a/(n-k).

nodes.name: r_k
nodes.statement: We define $r_k\in [0,\delta_k]$ as the value for which $|E^S_k| = (1-r_k)\cdot k\cdot (n-k)$.

nodes.name: Truncated random variables and caps c_k

For $k\in [s, n-s-1]$, let
\[
  \capped{X}^S_k := \min \{ X^S_k, c_k \} \quad\text{ and }\quad
  \capped{Y}^S_k := \sum_{i=s}^{k} \capped{X}^S_i, 
\]\[
\quad \text{ where } \quad
  c_{k} := \frac{2 \log{(\min\{ k, n-k\})} + \log \log{n}}{k(n-k) \cdot s^{-1/3}}.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Truncate each waiting time at c_k ≈ 2 log(min(k,n-k)) s^{1/3}/(k(n-k)); Ŷ sums the truncated waits.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement:
For every $k\in [s, n - s + 1]$ we define the function $w_k^{S}: E_k^{S} \rightarrow [0,1]$ as
  \[
  w^S_k(e) =
  \begin{cases}
    \lambda(e) - Y_{k-1}^{S}, & \quad \lambda(e) \geq Y_{k-1}^{S}\\
    \lambda(e) - Y_{k-1}^{S} + 1, & \quad \lambda(e) < Y_{k-1}^{S}.
  \end{cases}
  \]
  Notice that for any two edges $e,f \in E_k^{S}$ such that $\lambda(f) < Y_{k-1}^{S} \leq \lambda(e)$
  we have $w_k^{S}(e) < w_k^{S}(f)$. This together with the fact that the edge labels of $e_s^S,\ldots, e_{s+k+1}^S$ are increasing (see~\cref{lem:foremostTree}~(ii)) implies that $e_k^{S}$ is exactly
  the edge on which the minimum of $w_k^{S}$ is attained, that is,
  \begin{equation} e_k^{S}
    = \arg\min \{w_k^{S}(e) \mid e \in E_k^{S} \},
  \end{equation}
  and therefore, for every $k \in [s, n-s - 1]$,
  \begin{equation} X_k^{S}
    = \min\{w_k^{S}(e) \mid e \in E_k^{S}\}.
  \end{equation}
  Observe that upon exposure of edge $e_k^{S}$, we reveal some information about the time labels of the other edges in $E_k^{S}$.
  More precisely, we learn that these time labels are not contained in the interval $[Y_{k-1}^{S}, Y_k^{S}]$.
  Thus, if we inductively define the admissible range of $\lambda(e)$, $e \in E_k^{S}$, as
  \[
      I_k^{S}(e) :=
      \begin{cases}
        I_{k-1}^{S}(e) \setminus [Y_{k-2}^{S}, Y_{k-1}^{S}], & \quad e \in E_k^{S} \cap E_{k-1}^{S}\\
        [0,1], & \quad e \in E_k^{S} \setminus E_{k-1}^{S}
  \end{cases}
  \]
  then $\lambda(e)$ conditioned on $\mathcal A_{k-1}^{S}$ is uniformly distributed on $I_k^{S}(e)$.
  Let $\ell = \ell(e)$ be the unique index with $e \in E_\ell^{S} \setminus E_{\ell-1}^{S}$, i.e., the first iteration at which $e$ could have been added.
  Then we have $I_k^{S}(e) = [0,1] \setminus [Y_{\ell-1}^{S} , Y_{k-1}^{S}]$.
  It follows that $w_k^{S}(e)$ is uniformly distributed on its admissible range
  \[
    J_k^{S}(e) := \mathopen[ 0, Y_{\ell-1}^{S} - Y_{k-1}^{S} + 1 \mathclose]
  \]
  and clearly
    \begin{equation} \mathopen[ 0, 1 - Y_{k-1}^{S} \mathclose] \subseteq J_k^{S}(e) \subseteq [0, 1] \,.
  \end{equation}

  Note that $X_k^{S}$ is a minimum of $k(n-k)(1-r_k)$ independent random variables $w_k^{S}(e), e \in E_k^{S}$,
  where for every edge $e \in E_k^{S}$ the value $w_k^{S}(e)$ is distributed uniformly on its own
  admissible range $J_k^{S}(e)$. Recall also that $r_k\in[0,\delta_k]$.
  Let $X_k'$ be the minimum of $k(n-k)(1-r_k)$ independent random variables distributed uniformly on
  $\left[0, 1-Y_{k-1}^{S} \right]$, and $X_k''$ be the minimum of $k(n-k)(1-r_k)$ independent
  random variables distributed uniformly on $[0, 1]$.
  
  Then, the inclusion \eqref{eq:inclusion} implies
  \[
    \mathbb{P}[X_k' \geq t \mid Y_{k-1}^S] \leq \mathbb{P}[X_k^{S} \geq t \mid A_{k-1}^{S}] \leq \mathbb{P}[X_k'' \geq t],
    \]
  where $A_{k-1}^{S}$ is the event that specific
  edges $e^S_{s}, \ldots, e^S_{k-1}$ with time labels $Y^S_{s}, \ldots, Y^S_{k-1}$ are revealed in the
  first $k-s$ steps of the process. Therefore, by integrating and noting that
  the expected value of the minimum of $m$ independent variables distributed uniformly on $[0,a]$ is equal to $\frac{a}{m+1}$,
  we obtain
  \begin{equation}
    \begin{split}
      \frac{1-Y_{k-1}^{S}}{k(n-k) + 1}
      \leq
      \frac{1-Y_{k-1}^{S}}{k(n-k)(1-r_k) + 1}
      &=
      \mathbb{E}[ X_k' \mid Y_{k-1}^S]
      \\&\leq
      \mathbb{E}[ X_k^{S} \mid \mathcal A^v_{k-1}]
      \\&\leq
      \mathbb{E}[ X_k'']
      =
      \frac{1}{k(n-k)(1-r_k) + 1}
      \\&
      \leq
      \frac{1}{k(n-k)(1-\delta_k) + 1}.
    \end{split}
  \end{equation}

  To prove the second part of the lemma we first note that by definition $\capped{X}_k^{S} \leq X_k^{S}$, and hence
  \[
    \mathbb{E}[ \capped{X}_k^{S} \mid \mathcal A_{k-1}^{S} ]
    \leq
    \mathbb{E}[ X_k^{S} \mid \mathcal A_{k-1}^{S} ]
    \leq
    \frac{1}{k(n-k)(1-\delta_k) + 1}.
  \]
    Therefore, it remains to show the lower bound on $\mathbb{E}[ \capped{X}_k^{S} \mid \mathcal A_{k-1}^{S} ]$. For convenience, let us denote $M_k := k(n-k)(1-r_k)$.
  Then, we have
  \begin{equation*}
  \begin{split}
    \mathbb{E}[ \capped{X}_k^{S} \mid \mathcal A_{k-1}^{S} ]
    &=
    \int_{0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}[\capped{X}_k^{S} \geq t \mid A_{k-1}^{S}] d\! t
    =
    \int_{0}^{c_k} \mathbb{P}[\capped{X}_k^{S} \geq t \mid A_{k-1}^{S}] d\! t
    \\ &=
    \int_{0}^{c_k} \mathbb{P}[X_k^{S} \geq t \mid A_{k-1}^{S}] d\! t
    \geq
    \int_{0}^{c_k} \mathbb{P}[X_k' \geq t] d\! t
    \\ &=
    \int_{0}^{c_k} \left( 1 - \frac{t}{1 - Y_{k-1}^{S}} \right)^{M_k} d\! t
    \\ &=
    \frac{(1 - Y_{k-1}^{S}) + (c_k - (1 - Y_{k-1}^{S})) \left( 1 - \frac{c_k}{1 - Y_{k-1}^{S}} \right)^{M_k}}{M_k + 1}
    \\ & \geq
    \frac{(1 - Y_{k-1}^{S}) - (1 - Y_{k-1}^{S}) ( 1 - c_k )^{M_k}}{M_k + 1}
    \\ & =
    \frac{(1 - Y_{k-1}^{S}) \left( 1 - ( 1 - c_k )^{M_k} \right)}{M_k + 1},
  \end{split}
  \end{equation*}
    and the desired bound follows from the fact that
   $(1 - c_k)^{ k(n- k)(1-r_k)}  \leq (\log n)^{-s^{1/3}}$ following an analogous computation as in~\cref{eq:prob_capped_uncapped} and using that $\min\{k, n-k\}\ge s\ge \log n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement:
Let us fix $k\in [s, n - s - 1]$
  and define a martingale $Z^S_{s-1}, Z^S_{s}, \ldots, Z^S_{k}$ with $Z^S_{s-1}:= 0$ and
  \[
    Z_t^{S} := \capped{Y}_t^{S} - \sum_{i=s}^t \mathbb{E} [ \capped{X}_i^{S} \mid \mathcal A_{i-1}^{S} ]
         = \sum_{i=s}^t \capped{X}_i^{S} - \sum_{i=s}^t \mathbb{E}[\capped{X}_i^{S} \mid \mathcal A_{i-1}^{S}],
  \]
  for $t \in [s, k]$.

  Since $0 \leq \capped{X}_i^{S} \leq c_i$, we have
  $0 \leq \mathbb{E}[\capped{X}_i^{S} \mid \mathcal A_{i-1}^{S}] \leq c_i$,
  and therefore
  \[
  \mathbb{P}\left[\abs*{Z_{i}^{S}-Z_{i-1}^{S}}>c_i \right]
  =
  \mathbb{P}\left[ \abs*{\capped{X}_i^{S} - E[\capped{X}_i^{S} \mid\mathcal A_{i-1}^{S}]} >c_i\right]
  = 0
  \]
  holds for every $i\in [s, k]$.
  Furthermore, by \cref{lm:ck_bound}
  \[
    \sum_{i=s}^{k} c_i^2
    \leq
    \sum_{i=s}^{n-s-1} c_i^2
    \leq
    \frac{64 (\log \log{n})^2 (\log s)^2}{n^2s^{1/3}},
  \]
  and hence applying Azuma's inequality (\cref{the:Azuma}), we obtain that for sufficiently large $n$
  \begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
      \mathbb{P} \left[ |Z^S_k|\geq\frac{\log \log n}{n} \right]
      &\leq
      2\exp\left(
      \frac{-(\log \log n)^2}{n^2} \cdot
      \frac{1}{2\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_k^2}
      \right)
      \\ &\leq
      2\exp\left(
      \frac{-(\log \log n)^2}{n^2} \cdot
      \frac{n^2 s^{1/3}}{128 (\log \log{n})^2 (\log s)^2}
      \right)
      \\ &=
      2\exp\left(
      \frac{-s^{1/3}}{128 (\log s)^2}
      \right)
      \\ &\leq
      2\exp\left(\frac{-(\log n)^{b/3 - 2}}{128}\right)
      \\ &\leq
      n^{-\log n - 1},
    \end{split}
  \end{equation*}
  using that $b\ge 13$.
  The latter inequality together with the union bound over all $k\in [s, n-s-1]$ imply the desired result.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement:
Define $\gamma_1 := \frac{\log n}{\sqrt{n}}$.
  Recall that for each $k \in [s, n-s-1]$ we have
  \[
    e^S_k = \arg\min \{ w^S_k(e) \mid e \in E^S_k \},
  \]
  where the variable $w^S_k(e)$ is uniformly distributed on $J_k^S(e)$,
  which, by \eqref{eq:inclusion} and our assumption on $Y^S_{n-s-1}$, is an interval of the form $[0, w_e]$ with $1-\gamma_1 \le w_e \le 1$.
  Further recall that $|E^S_k|\in[(1-\delta_k)k (n-k),\, k(n-k)]$.
  
  Conditioned on $\mathcal A_{k-1}^S$, the probability~$p_e$ of the event~$e = e_S^v$ is then
  \begin{align*}
    p_e &= \int_{0}^{w_e} \frac{1}{w_e} \prod_{e' \in E^S_k \setminus \{e\}} \hspace{-2ex} \mathbb{P}[w^S_k(e') > x] d\! x
    = \int_{0}^{w_e} \frac{1}{w_e} \prod_{e' \in E^S_k \setminus \{e\}} \hspace{-2ex} \max\left\{0, \frac{w_{e'} - x}{w_{e'}}\right\} d\! x
    \\
    &\leq \int_0^1 \frac{1}{w_e} (1-x)^{\abs{E^S_k}-1} d\! x
    = \frac{1}{w_e \cdot \abs{E^S_k}} \leq \frac{1}{(1-\gamma_1) \cdot (1-\delta_k) \cdot k (n-k)}.
  \end{align*}
  On the other side, when setting $w_{\min} := \min\{w_e \mid e \in E^S_k\}$, then $p_e$~is lower-bounded by
  \begin{align*}
    p_e &\geq \int_0^{w_{\min}} \frac{1}{w_e} \left(\frac{w_{\min} - x}{w_{\min}}\right)^{\abs{E^S_k}-1} d\! x
    = \frac{w_{\min}}{w_e \cdot \abs{E^S_k}}
    \geq \frac{1-\gamma_1}{k (n-k)}.
  \end{align*}
  
  We now recall that each vertex $v$ has at most $(\log n)^a$ non-neighbors in the base graph $G$ and thus each vertex $u\in V\setminus V(\mathcal{G}_F^{k-1,S})$ has $n_u$ neighbors in $V(\mathcal{G}_F^{k-1,S})$, where
  \begin{align} k
    \ge n_u
    \ge k - (\log n)^a
    \ge k \cdot \Big(1 - \frac{(\log n)^a}{s}\Big)
    =: k \cdot (1-\gamma_3).
  \end{align}
  As
  $
    \mathbb{P}[u\in e_k^S \mid \mathcal A_{k-1}^S]
    = \sum_{e\in E\cap (V(\mathcal{G}_F^{k-1,S}\times \{u\}))} p_e
  $,
  by combining our bounds on~$p_e$ with~\eqref{eq:nubound}, we obtain
  \[
    (1-\gamma_1)(1-\gamma_3)\cdot \frac{1}{n-k}
    \le \mathbb{P}[u\in e_k^S \mid \mathcal A_{k-1}^S]
    \le \frac{1}{(1-\gamma_1)(1-\delta_k)}\cdot \frac{1}{n-k}.
  \]
  Notice now that
  \begin{align} (1-\gamma_1)(1-\gamma_3)\cdot \frac{1}{n-k}
    \ge (1 - \gamma_1 - \gamma_3)\cdot \frac{1}{n-k}
    \geq (1 - \gamma)\cdot \frac{1}{n-k}.
  \end{align}
  On the other hand, $\delta_k= \frac{(\log n)^a}{n - k}\le \frac{(\log n)^a}{s}=\gamma_3$ and thus
  \begin{align} \begin{split}
      \frac{1}{(1-\gamma_1)(1-\delta_k)}\cdot \frac{1}{n-k} 
      &\le \frac{1}{1-\gamma_1-\gamma_3} \cdot \frac{1}{n-k}
      \\ &\le \left(1 + 2(\gamma_1+\gamma_3) \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n-k}
      \\ &= (1 + \gamma) \cdot \frac{1}{n-k}.
    \end{split}
  \end{align}
  Now, \eqref{eq:uniformdown} and \eqref{eq:uniformup} together show the claim.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Assume for now that $Y_{n-s-1}^S \leq \frac{\log n}{\sqrt{n}}$.
  For $k\in [s, n - s - 1]$, let $P_k$ denote the event that the $k$-added vertex does not belong to $T$ and let $Q_k:=\bigcap_{i=s}^k P_i$ denote the event that all new vertices up to the $k$-added one do not belong to $T$.
  By~\cref{lem: almost uniform}, the $k$-added vertex is distributed almost uniformly on the vertices not reached yet.
  Thus, for $i\in [s, k]$, the probability that the $i$-added vertex belongs to $T$ conditioned on the events that the previous ones did not is $\mathbb{P}[\overline{P_i} \mid Q_{i-1}]\ge \frac{t\cdot(1-\gamma(n))}{n - i}\ge \frac{t}{2n}$ using the facts that $n-i\le n$ and $\gamma=\gamma(n)\le 1/2$ for $n$ large enough (see~\cref{lem: almost uniform} for the definition of $\gamma$).
  Hence, we get
  \begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}[Q_k]
    = \prod_{i=s}^k \mathbb{P}[P_i \mid Q_{i-1}]
    \le \left(1-\frac{t}{2n}\right)^{k - s}
  \end{align*}
  Let us now define $A$ as the event that
  $S$ can reach at least $d=\lceil n^z\rceil$ vertices. Using~\cref{lem: reachability} we obtain that $A$ occurs with probability at least $1-2n^{-\log \log n}$.
  Then, the probability that none of the new vertices belongs to $T$ conditioned on $A$ is
  \begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}[Q_k \mid A]
    &\le \left(1-\frac{t}{2n}\right)^{n^z-s}
    \le \exp\left(-\frac{t}{2n}\left(n^z-s\right)\right).
  \end{align*}
  In total we get $\mathbb{P}[Q_k]\le \mathbb{P}[Q_k\mid A] + \mathbb{P}[\overline A]\le 2n^{-\log\log n} + e^{-\frac{t}{2n}(n^z-s)}$.
  
  It remains to account for our initial assumption that~$Y_{n-s-1}^S \leq \frac{\log n}{\sqrt{n}}$,
  which fails to hold with probability at most $n^{-\frac{\log{n}}{4}}$ by \cref{cor: two hop}.
  Thus, the overall probability that the foremost forest algorithm does not reach~$T$
  is at most $2n^{-\log\log n} + e^{-\frac{t}{2n}(n^z-s)} + n^{-\frac{\log{n}}{4}} \leq \frac{5}{2}n^{-\log\log n} + e^{-\frac{t}{2n}(n^z-s)}$.

Let $c\in (0, 1)$ be any constant. With probability at least $1-2n^{-\sqrt{\log n}}$, for every vertex $v$, it holds that

    \left| \widehat{Y}_{\lceil c\cdot n \rceil}^v - \frac{\log n}{n}\right| \le \frac{3(\log n)^{0.8}}{n}.
  \]

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement:
By definition of the truncated variables, as $\widehat{Y}_{k}^v\leq Y_{k}^v$ for every $k\in [n-1]$, it holds also that $\widehat{Y}_{c\cdot n}^v\leq Y_{\lceil c\cdot n \rceil}^v$.
    Using \cref{cor: cn}, with probability at least $1-2n^{-\sqrt{\log n}}$, for every vertex $v$, it holds that
    \[
        Y_{\lceil c\cdot n \rceil}^v
        \geq \widehat{Y}_{\lceil c\cdot n \rceil}^v
        \geq\frac{\log n}{n}-\frac{3(\log n)^{0.8}}{n}.
    \]
    Hence, with probability at least $1-2n^{-\sqrt{\log n}}$,
    no vertex can reach $\lceil c\cdot n \rceil$ nodes
    in $\mathcal{G}$ when $p<\frac{\log n}{n}-\frac{3(\log n)^{0.8}}{n}$ and, thus, cannot be in a temporally connected component of size at least $c\cdot n$. Hence, there is no temporally connected component of size at least $c\cdot n $ in $\mathcal{G}$.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 11
nodes.statement:
The strategy is as follows (see also \cref{fig:proof_scheme}). We split the time interval $[0, p]$
into three intervals $I_{1}$, $I_{2}$, and $I_{3}$ of equal duration $p / 3$, and
reveal the edges of the graph in two phases.

In Phase 1, we reveal the edges whose
time labels are in one of the intervals $I_1$ and $I_3$. Using a result from~\cite{CasteigtsRRZ21} 
(\cref{lem: tree growth}), we can conclude that there are
$n - o(n)$ nodes (call them $X$), each of which \aas reaches at
least $\sqrt[3]{n}\log n$ vertices during $I_1$, and there are at least
$n - o(n)$ nodes (call them $Y$) that \aas is reached by at least $\sqrt[3]{n}\log n$
vertices during $I_3$.

In Phase 2, we reveal the edges appearing during the middle interval $I_2$.
We show that for every ordered pair of nodes $x,y$ in the set $Z := X \cap Y$ 
(which is our intended connected component), the set of vertices that $x$ can reach during $I_1$,
can reach during $I_2$ at least one vertex in the set of vertices that reach $y$ during $I_3$; thus
implying that $x$ can reach $y$ during $[0,p]$. For this purpose we can employ Theorem~\ref{theorem:general target set} with $S$ being the set that $x$ can reach during $I_1$ and $T$ being the set of vertices that can reach $y$ during $I_3$. Note that the analysis of this phase is what requires us to develop the generalization $\mathcal F_p(G)$ of the model $\mathcal F_{n,p}$. In fact, the static base graph $G$ used in the application of Theorem~\ref{theorem:general target set} is the graph obtained from $K_n$ by removing the edges that appeared during either $I_1$ or $I_3$. Finally, a union bound over all pairs of nodes $x$ and $y$ yields the result.
nodes.statement_short: Three-phase sketch: grow from x in I_1, into y in I_3, and connect the two sets in I_2 via the target-set theorem on F_p(G).

nodes.name: ε(n) = 1/log log n
nodes.statement: Throughout, we denote $\varepsilon(n):=\frac{1}{\log\log n}$.

nodes.name: Probability p for the upper bound
nodes.statement: Let $p=(1+\varepsilon(n))\cdot \frac{\log n}{n}$ and $\mathcal{G} \sim \mathcal{F}_{p}(K_n)$.

nodes.name: Interval endpoints p_i
nodes.statement: Our strategy is to split the interval $[0, p]$ into three sub-intervals $[p_0,p_1]$, $[p_1,p_2]$, $[p_2,p_3]$, where $p_i:=\frac{i}{3}(1+\varepsilon(n))\frac{\log n}{n}$ for $i\in[0, 3]$.

nodes.name: Reachability within one third of the time window
nodes.statement:
For $i\in [0, 2]$, the number of vertices \emph{reached by} (resp. \emph{reaching}) a fixed vertex in
  $\mathcal{G}_{[p_i,p_{i+1}]}$ lies within $[n^{1/3}\log n, n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}]$ with probability at least $1 - \frac{10}{\log n}$.
conclusions: the number of vertices \emph{reached by} (resp. \emph{reaching}) a fixed vertex in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_i,p_{i+1}]}$ lies within $[n^{1/3}\log n, n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}]$ with probability at least $1 - \frac{10}{\log n}$
nodes.label: cor: reach thirds

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5
nodes.statement:
We show the statement for $\mathcal{G}_{[0, p_1]}$, the other statements follow analogously via shifting the edge labels.
        We start with the lower bound. We apply~\cref{lem: tree growth}~(i) with $z(n)=\frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{\varepsilon(n)\log n}$ and $y=1$. We get that for large enough $n$ a fixed vertex in $\mathcal{G}\sim\mathcal{F}_{p}(K_n)$ can reach (resp. be reached by) at least
        \[
            \ceil*{\frac{n^z}{(\log n)^y}}
						\ge \frac{n^{\frac{1}{3} + \frac{2\log \log n}{\log n}}}{\log n}
            = n^{\frac{1}{3}} \log n
        \]
        nodes with probability at least $1-\frac{5}{\log n}$, if $p\ge p'(n)$, where $p'(n):=z \frac{\log n}{n} + 3 \frac{(\log n)^{0.8}}{n}$. Observe that
        \[
            p_1 \cdot n
            = \frac{1}{3}\cdot \log n + \frac{\varepsilon(n)}{3} \cdot \log n
            \ge \frac{1}{3}\cdot \log n + \frac{2}{\varepsilon(n)} + 3(\log n)^{0.8}
						= p'(n) \cdot n
        \]
				for sufficiently large $n$.

				In order to prove the upper bound, we apply~\cref{lem: tree growth}~(ii) with $z(n)=\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)$ and $y=1$. We get that for large enough $n$ a fixed vertex in $\mathcal{G}\sim\mathcal{F}_{p}(K_n)$ can reach (resp. be reached by) at most
        \[
            \ceil*{\frac{n^z}{(\log n)^y}}
						\le \frac{n^{\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)}}{\log n} + 1
						\le n^{\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)}
        \]
        nodes with probability at least $1-\frac{5}{\log n}$, if $p\le p'(n)$, where $p'(n):=z \frac{\log n}{n} - 3 \frac{(\log n)^{0.8}}{n}$. Observe that
        \[
            p_1 \cdot n
            = \Big(\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)\Big) \cdot \log n - \frac{2\varepsilon(n)}{3} \cdot\log n
            \le \Big(\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)\Big)\cdot  \log n - 3(\log n)^{0.8}
						= p'(n) \cdot n
        \]
				for sufficiently large $n$.

				We conclude by union bound that the cardinality of the set of vertices that a fixed vertex reaches (resp. is reached by) in $\mathcal{G}_{[0, p_1]}$ is in the wanted interval with probability at least $1-\frac{10}{\log n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply both parts of Lemma 10 with z = 1/3 + small corrections, check p_1 is on the right side, union bound.

nodes.name: Reduce to the first interval
nodes.statement: We show the statement for $\mathcal{G}_{[0, p_1]}$, the other statements follow analogously via shifting the edge labels.

nodes.statement:

nodes.statement:
In order to prove the upper bound, we apply~\cref{lem: tree growth}~(ii) with $z(n)=\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)$ and $y=1$. We get that for large enough $n$ a fixed vertex in $\mathcal{G}\sim\mathcal{F}_{p}(K_n)$ can reach (resp. be reached by) at most
        \[
            \ceil*{\frac{n^z}{(\log n)^y}}
						\le \frac{n^{\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)}}{\log n} + 1
						\le n^{\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)}
        \]
        nodes with probability at least $1-\frac{5}{\log n}$, if $p\le p'(n)$, where $p'(n):=z \frac{\log n}{n} - 3 \frac{(\log n)^{0.8}}{n}$. Observe that
        \[
            p_1 \cdot n
            = \Big(\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)\Big) \cdot \log n - \frac{2\varepsilon(n)}{3} \cdot\log n
            \le \Big(\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon(n)\Big)\cdot  \log n - 3(\log n)^{0.8}
						= p'(n) \cdot n

				for sufficiently large $n$.

nodes.name: Union bound over both bounds
nodes.statement: We conclude by union bound that the cardinality of the set of vertices that a fixed vertex reaches (resp. is reached by) in $\mathcal{G}_{[0, p_1]}$ is in the wanted interval with probability at least $1-\frac{10}{\log n}$.

nodes.name: Almost every vertex reaches many vertices
nodes.statement: Let $i\in \{0, 1, 2\}$. The number of vertices that can reach (resp. be reached by) at least $n^{1/3}\log n$ and at most $n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}$ vertices in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_i, p_{i+1}]}$ is at least $n - \frac{n}{\log \log n}$ with probability at least $1 - \frac{10 \log \log n}{\log n}$.
conclusions: The number of vertices that can reach (resp. be reached by) at least $n^{1/3}\log n$ and at most $n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}$ vertices in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_i, p_{i+1}]}$ is at least $n - \frac{n}{\log \log n}$ with probability at least $1 - \frac{10 \log \log n}{\log n}$
nodes.label: lemma: almost everyone reaches many

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 12
nodes.statement:
Let $\bar X$ denote the number of nodes in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_i, p_{i+1}]}$ that can reach (resp. be reached by) less than $n^{1/3}\log n$ or more than $n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}$ vertices in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_i, p_{i+1}]}$. Then $\mathbb{E}[\bar X] \le 10n /\log n$ by~\cref{cor: reach thirds}. Using Markov's inequality
        $
            \mathbb{P}\Big[\bar X \geq \frac{n}{\log\log n}\Big]
            \le \frac{10 \log \log n}{\log n}.
        $
nodes.statement_short: Expected number of bad vertices is at most 10n/log n by Corollary 5; Markov's inequality.

nodes.name: Count bad vertices
nodes.statement: Let $\bar X$ denote the number of nodes in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_i, p_{i+1}]}$ that can reach (resp. be reached by) less than $n^{1/3}\log n$ or more than $n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}$ vertices in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_i, p_{i+1}]}$. Then $\mathbb{E}[\bar X] \le 10n /\log n$ by~\cref{cor: reach thirds}.
nodes.statement_short: Count bad vertices; expectation from Corollary 5

nodes.name: Apply Markov's inequality
nodes.statement:
Using Markov's inequality
        $
            \mathbb{P}\Big[\bar X \geq \frac{n}{\log\log n}\Big]
            \le \frac{10 \log \log n}{\log n}.
        $
nodes.statement_short: Apply Markov's inequality

nodes.name: Sets X and Y of well-connected vertices
nodes.statement: We now denote by $X$ the set of nodes that can reach at least $n^{1/3}\log n$ and at most $n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}$ vertices in $\mathcal{G}_{[0, p_{1}]}$ and by $Y$ the set of nodes that are reached by at least $n^{1/3}\log n$ and at most $n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}$ vertices in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_2, p_{3}]}$.

nodes.name: Intersection Z = X ∩ Y
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we denote by $Z=X\cap Y$ their intersection.

nodes.name: Z is large
nodes.statement: According to~\cref{lemma: almost everyone reaches many}, it holds that $|Z|\ge n - \frac{2n}{\log \log n}$ with probability at least $1 - \frac{20 \log \log n}{\log n}$.
conclusions: $|Z|\ge n - \frac{2n}{\log \log n}$ with probability at least $1 - \frac{20 \log \log n}{\log n}$

nodes.name: Reach sets A(x) and B(y)
nodes.statement: To this end, let $A(x)$ be the set of nodes that $x$ can reach in $\mathcal{G}_{[0,p_1]}$ and let $B(y)$ be the set of nodes that can reach $y$ in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_2, p_3]}$.

nodes.name: Extended reach set A'(x)
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, for $x\in X$, let
\[
    A'(x):=\{v\in V: \exists a\in A(x) \text{ s.t.\ }a \text{ reaches } v \text{ in }\mathcal{G}_{[p_1, p_2]}\}
\]
be the set of nodes that $x$ can reach in $\mathcal{G}_{[0, p_2]}$.

nodes.name: x reaches y iff A'(x) meets B(y)
nodes.statement: Notice that $x$ reaches $y$ if and only if $A'(x)$ intersects $B(y)$.
conclusions: $x$ reaches $y$ if and only if $A'(x)$ intersects $B(y)$

nodes.name: Graphs G'' and G'
nodes.statement:
Let $G'' = (V, E'')$ with
$E'' = \{e \in \binom{V}{2} \mid \lambda(e) \in [0, p_1] \cup [p_2, p_3]\}$
be the graph containing all edges appearing in $\mathcal{G}_{[0, p_1]}$ or $\mathcal{G}_{[p_2, p_3]}$,
and let $G' = (V, E')$ with $E' = \binom{V}{2} \setminus E''$ contain all other edges.

nodes.name: A'(x) is distributed as a foremost forest in F_{p'}(G')
nodes.statement:
Then we observe that the distribution of the set $A'(x)$ conditioned on the information about the edges appearing in $\mathcal{G}_{[0,p_1]}$ and $\mathcal{G}_{[p_2, p_3]}$ is identical to the node set of a foremost forest grown from $S:=A(x)$ in $\mathcal{H}\sim \mathcal{F}_{p'}(G')$,
where $p'=\frac{1}{3}(1+\varepsilon(n))\frac{\log n}{n}$.
assumptions: conditioned on the information about the edges appearing in $\mathcal{G}_{[0,p_1]}$ and $\mathcal{G}_{[p_2, p_3]}$
conclusions: is identical to the node set of a foremost forest grown from $S:=A(x)$ in $\mathcal{H}\sim \mathcal{F}_{p'}(G')$
nodes.statement_short: Conditioned on edges of the outer thirds, A'(x) is a foremost forest from A(x) in F_{p'}(G') with p'=p/3.

nodes.name: G'' is an Erdős-Rényi graph
nodes.statement: Furthermore, $G''$ is distributed as an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} graph $G'' \sim G_{n, p}$ with $p:=\frac{2}{3}(1+\varepsilon(n))\frac{\log n}{n}$.
conclusions: $G''$ is distributed as an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} graph $G'' \sim G_{n, p}$

nodes.name: Degree bounds for G'' and G'
nodes.statement: It holds that $\Delta(G'')\le 4\log n$ a.a.s.\ and, thus, $\delta(G')\ge n - (\log n)^2$ a.a.s.
conclusions: $\Delta(G'')\le 4\log n$ a.a.s.
$\delta(G')\ge n - (\log n)^2$ a.a.s.
nodes.label: obs: min degree

nodes.name: Proof of Observation 1
nodes.statement:
Recall that $G''$ is distributed according to $G_{n, p}$ with $p:=\frac{2}{3}(1+\varepsilon(n))\frac{\log n}{n}$. Following~\cite[Corollary 3.13]{Bollobas2001}, with $m=1$ and $\omega(n)=\log n$, we have that a.a.s.\
	\[
			\Delta(G'') \leq pn + \sqrt{2pn\log n} + \log n \sqrt{\frac{pn}{\log n}}
			\le \log n + \sqrt{2 (\log n)^2} + \log n
			\le 4 \log n.
	\]
	The observation about the minimum degree now follows immediately for sufficiently large $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the standard maximum-degree bound for G_{n,p} (Bollobás, Cor. 3.13).

nodes.name: Recall G'' ~ G_{n,p}
nodes.statement: Recall that $G''$ is distributed according to $G_{n, p}$ with $p:=\frac{2}{3}(1+\varepsilon(n))\frac{\log n}{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall G'' ~ G_{n,p}

nodes.statement:
Following~\cite[Corollary 3.13]{Bollobas2001}, with $m=1$ and $\omega(n)=\log n$, we have that a.a.s.\
	\[
			\Delta(G'') \leq pn + \sqrt{2pn\log n} + \log n \sqrt{\frac{pn}{\log n}}
			\le \log n + \sqrt{2 (\log n)^2} + \log n
			\le 4 \log n.

	The observation about the minimum degree now follows immediately for sufficiently large $n$.

nodes.name: Target-set reachability for polynomial-size sets
nodes.statement:
Let
  \begin{itemize}
    \item $G$ be a graph of minimum degree $\delta(G)\ge n - (\log n)^a$ for some $a\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$,
    \item let $S$ and $T$ be two sets of nodes in $G$, each of cardinality at least $n^{1/3}\log n$, and
    \item let $\mathcal{G}\sim \mathcal{F}_{p}(G)$ with $p\ge \frac{1}{3}(1+\varepsilon(n))\frac{\log n}{n}$.
  \end{itemize}
  Then, the foremost forest algorithm from $S$ on $\mathcal{G}$ reaches $T$ with probability at least $1-3n^{-\log\log n}$.
assumptions: $G$ be a graph of minimum degree $\delta(G)\ge n - (\log n)^a$ for some $a\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$
$S$ and $T$ be two sets of nodes in $G$, each of cardinality at least $n^{1/3}\log n$
conclusions: the foremost forest algorithm from $S$ on $\mathcal{G}$ reaches $T$ with probability at least $1-3n^{-\log\log n}$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 6
nodes.statement_short: Check p meets the hypothesis of Theorem 1 with z = 2/3 + 2 log log n/log n and evaluate the bound.

nodes.name: Fix sizes
nodes.statement:
Set $s := \abs{S}$, $t := \abs{T}$.
	Without loss of generality, we may assume $s \leq n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix sizes; WLOG s small

nodes.name: p satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Note that for large enough $n$ it holds that
	\begin{align*}
		p
    &\ge \frac{1}{3}\Big(1+\frac{1}{\log \log n}\Big)\frac{\log n}{n}\\
    &\ge \frac{\frac{1}{3}\log n + 4 \log \log n}{n}\\
    &= \frac{\frac{2}{3}\log n + 2 \log \log n - \frac{1}{3}\log n - \log \log n}{n} + \frac{3\log \log n}{n}\\
    &\ge \frac{z\log n - \log s}{n} + \frac{3\log \log n}{n},
	\end{align*}
  for $z = \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2\log\log n}{\log n}$.
nodes.statement_short: p satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 1 and simplify
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 1 and simplify

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 11
nodes.statement:
Let $p= (1+\varepsilon(n))\cdot \frac{\log n}{n}$ and $\mathcal{G} \sim \mathcal{F}_{p}(K_n)$. As above, let $X$ be the nodes that can reach between $n^{1/3}\log n$ and $n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}$ vertices in $\mathcal{G}_{[0, p_{1}]}$ and let $Y$ be the nodes that are reached by between $n^{1/3}\log n$ and $n^{1/3 + \varepsilon(n)}$ vertices in $\mathcal{G}_{[p_2, p_{3}]}$.
	Furthermore, let $Z=X\cap Y$ be their intersection and recall that $|Z|\ge n - \frac{2n}{\log \log n}$ with probability at least $1 - \frac{20 \log \log n}{\log n}$ according to~\cref{lemma: almost everyone reaches many}.
	Now, conditioned on the information about the edges appearing in $\mathcal{G}_{[0,p_1]}$ and $\mathcal{G}_{[p_2, p_3]}$, let $G'=(V, E')$ be the static graph with the same node set as $\mathcal{G}$ and the edge set $E'=\{e\in \binom{V}{2}:\lambda(e)\notin [p_0, p_1]\cup [p_2, p_3]\}$, where $\lambda$ is the time label function of $\mathcal{G}$.

nodes.statement:
Thus, it remains to prove the upper bound.
  We employ our strategy of splitting the time into three intervals. 
  We do not need to make any changes to our approach in the middle one (Phase 2), which previously required the most effort.
  However, we now need to do additional work in the first and last interval (Phase 1), which is the main technical contribution of this part.
  Recall that in the proof of \cref{thm: upper bound}, we only required that $n-o(n)$~vertices can all reach (resp.\ be reached by) at least $n^{1/3} \log n$~vertices within each of the three intervals from Figure~\ref{fig:proof_scheme}.

  such that every vertex in this set can reach (resp.\ be reached by) at least $n^{1/3}\log n$~vertices \emph{via temporal paths that use only vertices in~$V'$}. Once this is achieved, we can use the same approach as in the case of open components for Phase 2.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 5 (part 2)
nodes.statement:
In order to obtain the set of vertices $V'$ mentioned above, we have to insert an additional Phase 1.1,
  which looks only at a short time interval~$I_1$ at the very beginning (and symmetrically $I_5$ at the very end).
  The purpose of this new phase is to ``bootstrap'' the closed component by identifying a set~$V'$ of $n' = n - o(n)$~vertices,
  which each reach at least \emph{poly-logarithmically} many vertices by paths that are contained in~$V'$.
  \Cref{lm:bootstrap-reachability} formalizes this result.
  
  A technical difficulty in Phase 1.1 is the need to control possible cascading effects,
  where removing low-degree vertices from the graph can cause further vertices to become low-degree vertices, etc.
  We overcome this difficulty by partitioning the vertices into sets $V_1, \dots, V_C$, which we refer to as \emph{sectors}, and removing vertices from each sector~$V_i$ solely on the base of whether they have too few neighbors in the \emph{next sector}~$V_{i+1}$.
  This ensures that the sets of vertices removed from each sector are determined independently of each other.
  On this base, we are then able to prove that no cascading effects occur a.a.s.
  Subsequently, we show that after these removals, every remaining vertex can reach a poly-logarithmic number of others by considering \emph{clocked} paths, which essentially march in lockstep, traversing the sectors in circular order (see \cref{fig:sectors}).
  
  Subsequently, in Phase 1.2, we reveal edges that appear during $I_2$ or $I_4$. 
  We use the foremost forest technique developed earlier to show that,
  conditioned on the edges revealed in Phase 1.1, for every vertex $v$ in $V'$ the poly-logarithmic set of
  vertices reached by~$v$ during~$I_1$ reaches \emph{polynomially many} (by which we mean $n^p$ for some fixed $p<1$) vertices during~$I_2$. (Similarly,
  the set of vertices that reach~$v$ during~$I_5$ is reached by polynomially many 
  vertices during $I_4$.)

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5
nodes.statement:
Let $\gamma=0.7$, $\alpha=0.9$, $C = 30$,
	and let $n'(n) \in n-o(n)$ be the size of the vertex set guaranteed by \cref{lm:bootstrap-reachability}.
	Set $\varepsilon_1 := C^2 \frac{(\log n)^\alpha}{n} \in o\pfrac{\log n}{n}$,
	$\varepsilon_2 := 4\frac{\log \log n'}{\log n'} \in o(1)$, and
	$\varepsilon_3 := \frac{1}{3\log \log n} \in o(1)$.
	Set also $p_1 := \left(\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon_2\right) \frac{\log n'}{n'}$ and 
	$p_2 := \left(\frac{1}{3} + \varepsilon_3\right) \frac{\log n'}{n'}$.
	Finally, define 
	$
	p := 2\varepsilon_1 + 2p_1 + p_2,
	$
	which is equal to $\frac{\log n}{n} + \varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon \in o\pfrac{\log n}{n}$.
	
	
	Let $\mathcal G \sim \mathcal F_{n,p}$. We split $[0,p]$
	into a total of five intervals $I_i$, $i \in [5]$. The first and the last interval are short and each has length $\varepsilon_1$, i.e., $I_1 = [0, \varepsilon_1]$ and $I_5 = [p-\varepsilon_1, p]$. The three middle intervals are long
	and have lengths $p_1, p_2$, and $p_1$, respectively, i.e., $I_2=[\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_1 + p_1]$,
	$I_3 = [\varepsilon_1 + p_1, \varepsilon_1 + p_1 + p_2]$, $I_4 = [p - (\varepsilon_1 + p_1), p-\varepsilon_1]$.
	We will reveal the edges of the graph in three phases (Phase 1.1, Phase, 1.2, and Phase 2), as was graphically summarized in \cref{fig:closed_component_three_phases} in the introduction, and in each phase we condition on the edges revealed in the previous phases. In Phase 1.1 we reveal edges in the intervals $I_1$ and
	$I_5$ and apply \cref{lm:bootstrap-reachability} to identify a large set of nodes $V'$, each of which can reach poly-logarithmically many vertices in $V'$ during the first interval and can be reached by poly-logarithmically many vertices in $V'$ during the last interval via temporal paths that use only nodes from $V'$. In the subsequent phases we restrict our attention to the subgraph induced by $V'$, which is the target giant closed connected component.
	In Phase 1.2, we reveal edges appearing in the intervals $I_2$ and $I_4$. Because in 
	Phase 1.1 \aas we revealed poly-logarithmic number of edges for every vertex, we can use \cref{lem: reachability} to argue that for every vertex $v \in V'$ the poly-logarithmic set of vertices reached by $v$ during $I_1$ can reach polynomially many vertices during $I_2$. Similarly, during $I_4$ polynomially many
	vertices can reach the poly-logarithmic set of vertices that reach $v$ during $I_5$. The main outcome of this phase is that every vertex in $v \in V'$ reaches polynomially many vertices in $V'$ during $I_1 \cup I_2$ and is reached by at least as many vertices in $I_4 \cup I_5$. 
	Finally, in Phase 2, because in the previous phases \aas at most poly-logarithmically many
	edges were revealed for every vertex, we can apply \cref{corollary: target set} to prove that for each ordered pair of vertices $u,w \in V'$ the set of vertices reached by $u$ during $I_1 \cup I_2$ can reach during $I_3$ the set of vertices that reach $w$ during $I_4 \cup I_5$, implying that $u$ can reach $w$ during $[0,p]$. We now proceed with the formal details.
		
	
	\paragraph*{Phase 1.1.}
	Let $\mathcal G_1$ be the temporal subgraph of $\mathcal G$ formed by the edges with time labels in the intervals $I_1 \cup I_5$. Note that, up to shifting the time labels in the interval $I_5$ by
	$p - 2\varepsilon_1$, $\mathcal G_1$ is distributed according to $\mathcal F_{n, 2\varepsilon_1}$.
	Thus, by \cref{lm:bootstrap-reachability}, \aas there is a set $V' \subseteq V(\mathcal G)$ containing
	$n'$ vertices such that, denoting $\mathcal G' := \mathcal G[V']$, every vertex $v \in V'$ 
	reaches a set $R_1(v)$ of at least $(\log n)^{(C-3)\gamma}$~vertices in $\mathcal G'_{I_1}$ and
	is reached by a set $R_1'(v)$ of at least $(\log n)^{(C-3)\gamma}$~vertices in $\mathcal G'_{I_5}$.
	
	\paragraph*{Phase 1.2.}
	Let $G_1$ be the underlying graph of $\mathcal G_1$. 
	Since $G_1$ is distributed as an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} graph $G_{n,\,2\varepsilon_1}$,
	similarly to \cref{obs: min degree}, we have that $\Delta(G_1) < 4 \log n$ a.a.s.
	Hence, in the graph $G_2' = \left(V', {V' \choose 2} \setminus E(G_1) \right)$ the minimum degree is at least $n' - 4 \log n \geq n' - (\log n')^2$.
	Observe that, up to shifting time labels, $\mathcal G'_{I_2} \sim \mathcal F_{p_1}(G_2')$ when conditioning on the knowledge about all edges seen in $I_1 \cup I_5$.
	
	Therefore, since $\abs{R_1(v)} \geq (\log n')^{13}$ for every vertex $v \in V'$, by applying
	\cref{lem: reachability} to $\mathcal G'_{I_2}$ and $R_1(v)$ 
	(with parameter $z = 1/3 + \frac{\log \log n'}{\log n'}$), we conclude that
	the vertices in $R_1(v)$ reach in $\mathcal G'_{I_2}$ at least $r := {(n')}^{\frac{1}{3} + \frac{\log\log n'}{\log n'}} = (n')^{1/3} \log n'$ vertices with probability at least $1-2(n')^{-\log\log n'}$.
	By the union bound, we have that with probability at least $1-2(n')^{1-\log\log n'} \in 1-o(1)$, every vertex $v \in V'$ can reach in $\mathcal G'_{I_1 \cup I_2}$ a set $R_2(v)$ of at least $r$ vertices.
	Symmetrically, with probability at least $1-2(n')^{1-\log\log n'} \in 1-o(1)$, every vertex $v \in V'$ is reached in $\mathcal G'_{I_4 \cup I_5}$ by a set~$R_2'(v)$ of at least $r$ vertices.
	
	\paragraph*{Phase 2.}
	Let $G_3'$ be the static graph defined by the vertex set $V'$ and all edges appearing in $\mathcal G'_{I_1 \cup I_2}$ and $\mathcal G'_{I_4 \cup I_5}$. As in Phase 1.2, we can argue that the maximum degree of $G_3'$ is at most $4 \log n'$ \aas, and therefore the minimum degree of the graph $G_4' = \left(V', {V' \choose 2} \setminus E(G_3') \right)$ 
	is at least $n' - (\log n')^2$. Hence, up to shifting time labels, $\mathcal G'_{I_3}$ is distributed according to $\mathcal F_{p_2}(G_4')$ when conditioned on the knowledge of all edges revealed in $I_1 \cup I_2 \cup I_4 \cup I_5$.
	
	Thus, by \cref{corollary: target set}, a given set of at least $(n')^{1/3} \log n'$ vertices in $\mathcal G'_{I_3}$ can reach another given set of at least as many vertices with probability at least $1-3(n')^{-\log\log n'}$. Applying this to all ordered pairs of sets $(R_2(v), R'_2(w))$, $v, w \in V'$ and
	using the union bound, we conclude that
	the probability that all these pairs of sets reach each other in $\mathcal G'_{I_3}$ is at least $1-3(n')^{2-\log\log n'} \in 1-o(1)$.
	
	Putting all together, we conclude that \aas in $\mathcal G' = \mathcal G[V']$ any vertex reaches every other vertex.
	Thus, $V'$ is, as desired, a giant closed connected component.

nodes.name: Chernoff bounds
nodes.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots, X_T$ be independent random variables taking values in $\{0,1\}$, let $X$ denote their sum, and let $\mu=\mathbb{E}[X]$. Then, the following hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item For any $\delta>0$,
    \[
      \mathbb{P}[X\ge (1+\delta) \mu] 
      \le \Big( \frac{e^\delta}{(1+\delta)^{1+\delta}} \Big)^\mu
      \le \exp\Big(-\frac{\mu \delta^2}{2+\delta}\Big).
    \]
    \item For any $R\ge 6\mu$,
    \[
      \mathbb{P}[X\ge R] \le 2^{-R}.
    \]
    \item For any $0<\delta<1$,
    \[
      \mathbb{P}[X\le (1-\delta) \mu] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{\mu \delta^2}{2}\Big).
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $X_1,\ldots, X_T$ be independent random variables taking values in $\{0,1\}$
nodes.label: lem: chernoff

nodes.name: Balanced vertex partition V_1,...,V_C
nodes.statement:
To this end, we fix a random \emph{balanced} partition $V_1 \cup V_2 \cup \ldots \cup V_C$
of the vertex set $V$ of $\mathcal G$ into $C$ parts ('balanced' means that each part has size either $\lceil n/C \rceil$ or $\lfloor n / C \rfloor$); this partition is independent of $\mathcal G$.
differentia: each part has size either $\lceil n/C \rceil$ or $\lfloor n / C \rfloor$

nodes.name: Time subintervals T_i and D = 2C
nodes.statement:
We also split the time interval $[0,p]$ into $D := 2C$ 
equal subintervals $T_i$, $i \in [D]$, where $T_i := [(i-1)p/D,\; ip/D]$.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 13
nodes.statement:
We will identify subsets $V_i' \subseteq V_i$ such that $|V_i \setminus V_i'| \in o(n)$ 
and for every vertex $v \in V_i'$ we will construct a reachability
tree rooted at $v$ with the desired number of vertices.
Such a tree will have a special structure. Namely,
(i) the $k$-th level of the tree will be entirely in $V_{i+k}'$ 
(for convenience, indices are taken modulo $C$, i.e., $V_{C+1} = V_1$, etc.); and (ii) the time labels of the edges connecting the tree vertices at level $k-1$ with the tree vertices at level $k$ will belong to the $k$-th time interval $T_k$. 
This construction will use the first $C$ time intervals. The last $C$ time intervals will be used in a similar way
to construct reachability trees witnessing that every vertex in $V' := \cup_{i \in [C]} V_i'$ is reachable by the desired number of vertices in $V'$. The argument for the later is the same up to going backward in time, so we provide details only for the first half of the time intervals.
nodes.statement_short: Build layered reachability trees through sectors V'_{i+k} using edges of time slot T_k; backward in time for reachedness.

nodes.statement: Furthermore, each such underlying graph is an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} graph $G_{n,p/D}$.
conclusions: each such underlying graph is an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} graph $G_{n,p/D}$

nodes.name: Multi-epoch expected neighbours
assumptions: $G_1, G_2, \ldots, G_D \sim G_{n, \frac{p}{D}}$ be, not necessarily independent, Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi{} graphs on the common vertex set~$V$
conclusions: $|V_i\setminus V_i'|\in o(n)$
in every $G_j$, $j \in [D]$, every vertex in~$V_i'$ has at least $(\log n)^\gamma$ neighbours in $V'_{i+1}$

nodes.name: Few collisions
nodes.statement:
Let $U$ and $W$ be any two fixed parts of the partition $\{ V_i \}_{i \in [C]}$.
	Let $G \sim G_{n, \frac{p}{D}}$ and let $A \subseteq U$ be a set of size 
	at most $(\log n)^{C\gamma}$, chosen independently from the edges of $G$ between $U$ and $W$.
	Then, with probability at least $1-o(1/n)$, in graph $G$ no vertex in $W$ has three neighbors in $A$
	and at most one vertex has two neighbors in $A$.
assumptions: $U$ and $W$ be any two fixed parts of the partition $\{ V_i \}_{i \in [C]}$
$A \subseteq U$ be a set of size at most $(\log n)^{C\gamma}$, chosen independently from the edges of $G$ between $U$ and $W$
conclusions: with probability at least $1-o(1/n)$, in graph $G$ no vertex in $W$ has three neighbors in $A$ and at most one vertex has two neighbors in $A$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13
nodes.statement:
Let $G_i$ be the underlying graph of $\mathcal G_{T_i}$, $i \in [D]$. Then all these underlying graphs 
	are distributed according to $G_{n,p/D}$ and, thus, by~\cref{lm:multi-epoch-expected-neighbours} \aas there are subsets $V'_i \subseteq V_i$, $i \in [C]$ satisfying the properties stated in the same lemma.

	
	Consider some $v\in V'_i$, and let $\ell \in [C]$.
	A temporal path in $\mathcal G$ starting at~$v$ is a \emph{clocked path from $v$ of length $\ell$}
	if for every~$j \in [\ell]$ the~$j$-th edge of the path 
	connects a vertex in $V'_{i+j-1}$ with a vertex in $V'_{i+j}$,
	and its time label belongs to $T_j$ (i.e., the edge belongs to $G_j$).
	We will prove that \aas clocked paths from $v$ of length at most $C$ reach at least 
	$(\log n)^{(C-3)\gamma}$ vertices.
	
	Assume this is not the case.
	Then we will show by induction that clocked paths from $v$ of length $j \in [C]$ reach at least $(\log n)^{(j-1)\gamma} +1$ vertices in $V'_{i+j}$, leading to a contradiction as the clocked paths from $v$ of length at most $C-2$ would suffice to reach the desired number of vertices.
	
	The base case where $j=1$ is immediate, since in $G_1$ vertex $v$~has at least $(\log n)^\gamma \geq 2$~neighbors in~$V'_{i+1}$.
	
	For the induction step, let $A'\subseteq V'_{i+j}$ be the set of vertices reached by~$v$ via clocked paths of length~$j$.
	By the induction hypothesis, $\abs{A'} \geq (\log n)^{(j-1)\gamma}+1$.
	In graph $G_{j+1}$, each of the vertices of~$A'$ has at least $(\log n)^\gamma$~edges to $V'_{i+j+1}$,
	and each of these edges then completes a clocked path from $v$ of length~$j+1$.
	If there were no collisions (i.e., multiple edges leading to the same vertex in~$V'_{i+j+1}$),
	then $v$~would thus reach $(\log n)^{j\gamma}+(\log n)^\gamma$ 
	vertices in~$V'_{i+j+1}$, which is more than enough. It remains to bound the number of collisions.
	
	Ideally, we would like to apply \cref{lm:few-collisions} to~$A'$.
	However, in the proof of \cref{lm:multi-epoch-expected-neighbours}, the set $V'_{i+j}$ (and thus~$A'$) was selected based on the edges of the graphs $G_s$, $s \in [D]$, between $V_{i+j}$ and~$V_{i+j+1}$, thus violating the independence assumption of \cref{lm:few-collisions}.
	To remedy this, let $B' \subseteq V_{i+j-1}'$ contain all vertices reached from~$v$ via clocked paths of length~$j-1$ and let $A \subseteq V_{i+j}$ contain all those vertices that are connected to~$B'$ in~$G_j$.
	Then clearly $A \cap V'_{i+j} = A'$, and the choice of~$A$ is now independent of the edges between $V_{i+j}$ and~$V_{i+j+1}$ in any of the graphs $G_s$, $s \in [D]$.
	By our assumption above, $\abs{B'} < (\log n)^{(C-3)\gamma}$.
	Thus, $\mathbb{E}[\abs{A}] < (\log n)^{(C-3)\gamma + \alpha} + 1 \leq (\log n)^{(C-1)\gamma}$.
  By a Chernoff bound (Lemma~\ref{lem: chernoff}~\emph{(\ref{chernoff 2})}) and using $(\log n)^{C\gamma} > 6\mathbb{E}[\abs{A}]$, we have
	\[
	\mathbb{P}\left[\abs{A} > (\log n)^{C \gamma}\right] < 2^{-(\log n)^{C \gamma}} \in o(1/n).
	\]
	Thus, with probability $1-o(1/n)$, we may apply \cref{lm:few-collisions} to $A$ and $G_{j+1}$ to conclude that in $G_{j+1}$ there is at most one collision between all edges leading from~$A$ to~$V_{i+j+1}$.
	Since $A' \subseteq A$ and $V'_{i+j+1} \subseteq V_{i+j+1}$, the same then holds for the edges from~$A'$ to~$V'_{i+j+1}$.
	In other words, $A'$~has at least $(\log n)^{j\gamma}+(\log n)^\gamma -1 \geq (\log n)^{j\gamma} +1$ neighbors in $V'_{i+j+1}$ in graph $G_{j+1}$, and thus the induction step succeeds with probability $1-o(1/n)$.
	
	By the union bound, this argument holds simultaneously for all~$j \in [C]$ and every possible choice of~$v \in V'$ a.a.s.
	This concludes the proof that \aas in $\mathcal{G}[V']$ every vertex reaches at least $(\log n)^{C-3}\gamma$~vertices during the first~$C$~time intervals, i.e., during $[0,p/2]$.
	The second part of the claim is proven analogously, now going backward in time but still in the same direction through the parts of the partition.
nodes.statement_short: Clocked paths through sectors grow by a (log n)^γ factor per layer; few collisions (Lemma 16) keep growth, by induction.

By the union bound, this argument holds simultaneously for all~$j \in [C]$ and every possible choice of~$v \in V'$ a.a.s.
	This concludes the proof that \aas in $\mathcal{G}[V']$ every vertex reaches at least $(\log n)^{C-3}\gamma$~vertices during the first~$C$~time intervals, i.e., during $[0,p/2]$.

nodes.name: Parameter β and fixed parts U, W
nodes.statement:
Let $\beta$ be such that $\gamma<\beta<\alpha$, and
let $U$ and $W$ be two arbitrary but fixed parts of the balanced partition $\{ V_i \}_{i \in [C]}$.

nodes.name: Few sleepers
nodes.statement:
In $G \sim G_{n, \frac{p}{D}}$ \aas
	at most $n \exp\left(-(\log n)^\alpha/12\right)$ vertices in $U$ have fewer than $(\log n)^\beta$ neighbours in $W$.
conclusions: at most $n \exp\left(-(\log n)^\alpha/12\right)$ vertices in $U$ have fewer than $(\log n)^\beta$ neighbours in $W$
nodes.label: lm:few-sleepers

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 17
nodes.statement:
For any vertex~$u \in U$, its number~$\partial(u)$ of neighbours in~$W$
	is the sum of $|W|$ indicator variables.
	Thus, 
	$\mathbb{E}[\partial(u)] = |W| \frac{p}{D}\geq
	\left\lfloor\frac{n}{C}\right\rfloor C \frac{(\log n)^\alpha}{n} 
	>\frac{1}{2}(\log n)^\alpha$.
	Using a Chernoff bound (Lemma~\ref{lem: chernoff}~\emph{(\ref{chernoff 3})}),
	\begin{align*}
		\mathbb{P}[\partial(u) < (\log n)^\beta]
		&< \exp \left( - \frac{\mathbb{E}[\partial(u)]}{2} \left(1-\frac{(\log n)^\beta}{\mathbb{E}[\partial(u)]}\right)^2 \right)
		\\ &< \exp \left( - \frac{\mathbb{E}[\partial(u)]}{3}\right)
		< \exp \left( - \frac{(\log n)^\alpha}{6} \right).
	\end{align*}
	
	As the edges to~$W$ for different $u \in U$ are independent,
	we can further apply a Chernoff bound to estimate the number of vertices with fewer than $(\log n)^\beta$ neighbours.
	For this purpose, let $S=\{u \in U \mid  \partial(u) < (\log n)^\beta\}$.
	Then $\mathbb{E}[\abs{S}]<\left\lceil \frac{n}{C} \right\rceil \cdot \exp \left( - \frac{(\log n)^\alpha}{6}\right)$, and
	by denoting $\delta := \frac{n \exp \left( - \frac{(\log n)^\alpha}{12} \right)}{\mathbb{E}[\abs{S}]}-1 \in \omega(1)$,
	using a Chernoff bound (Lemma~\ref{lem: chernoff}~\emph{(\ref{chernoff 1})}) gives 
	\begin{align*}
		\mathbb{P}\left[\abs{S}>n\cdot \exp \left( - \frac{(\log n)^\alpha}{12}\right) \right]
		&=
		\mathbb{P}[\abs{S}>(1+\delta)\mathbb{E}[\abs{S}]]
		\\&<
		\exp\left(-\frac{\delta^2 \mathbb{E}[\abs{S}]}{2+ \delta}\right)
		<
		\exp\left(-\frac{(1+\delta) \mathbb{E}[\abs{S}]}{2}\right)
		\\ &=
		\exp\left(-\frac{n\exp \left(- \frac{(\log n)^\alpha}{12} \right)}{2}\right)
		\in o\left( \exp\left(-\sqrt{n}\right)\right),
	\end{align*}
	which implies the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff for each vertex's degree into W, then Chernoff again for the number of low-degree vertices.
